stem: A 52-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance, and pallor for 3 months. Lab results show microcytic, hypochromic anemia with low ferritin and high TIBC, consistent with iron deficiency anemia. He denies NSAID use and has no history of chronic kidney disease. Which underlying cause should be considered most likely in this adult male?

B.title: Gastrointestinal bleeding (ulcer/malignancy)
B.body:
In adult males (and post-menopausal women), iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is considered a sign of pathological blood loss until proven otherwise. The most common source of chronic, occult blood loss in this demographic is the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
Occult Blood Loss: GI bleeding from sources like peptic ulcers, gastritis, or, most importantly, colorectal cancer or gastric cancer, can be slow and chronic. This slow loss is often asymptomatic and is the primary mechanism that depletes the body's iron stores, leading to IDA.
Age and Sex: Given the patient's age (52) and sex (male), common physiologic causes like menstruation are excluded, making a GI pathology—which becomes more prevalent with age—the leading differential diagnosis.
Workup must include stool occult blood test and upper/lower GI endoscopy to rule out malignancy because IDA in adult men is considered colon cancer until proven otherwise.
B.bodyHtml:
In adult males (and post-menopausal women), iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is considered a sign of pathological blood loss until proven otherwise. The most common source of chronic, occult blood loss in this demographic is the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.

  • Occult Blood Loss: GI bleeding from sources like peptic ulcers, gastritis, or, most importantly, colorectal cancer or gastric cancer, can be slow and chronic. This slow loss is often asymptomatic and is the primary mechanism that depletes the body's iron stores, leading to IDA.
  • Age and Sex: Given the patient's age (52) and sex (male), common physiologic causes like menstruation are excluded, making a GI pathology—which becomes more prevalent with age—the leading differential diagnosis.
  • Workup must include stool occult blood test and upper/lower GI endoscopy to rule out malignancy because IDA in adult men is considered colon cancer until proven otherwise.

A.title: Menorrhagia
A.body:
Heavy menstrual bleeding is the most common cause of IDA in reproductive-age women, not men.
Not applicable to male patients.
A.bodyHtml:
• Heavy menstrual bleeding is the most common cause of IDA in reproductive-age women, not men.
  • Not applicable to male patients.

C.title: Poor dietary intake
C.body:
Diet-related iron deficiency is rare in adult men because daily iron needs are low and diet typically provides enough iron.
Usually contributes only in strict vegetarians or malnutrition, but still far less common than GI blood loss.
C.bodyHtml:
• Diet-related iron deficiency is rare in adult men because daily iron needs are low and diet typically provides enough iron.
  • Usually contributes only in strict vegetarians or malnutrition, but still far less common than GI blood loss.

D.title: Pregnancy
D.body:
Causes increased iron demand and volume expansion–related anemia in women.
Not relevant to an adult male patient.
D.bodyHtml:
• Causes increased iron demand and volume expansion–related anemia in women.
  • Not relevant to an adult male patient.

E.title: Celiac disease
E.body:
Can cause malabsorption leading to IDA, but it is far less common than chronic GI bleeding in older men.
Considered when anemia persists despite iron therapy or other autoimmune symptoms appear.
E.bodyHtml:
• Can cause malabsorption leading to IDA, but it is far less common than chronic GI bleeding in older men.
  • Considered when anemia persists despite iron therapy or other autoimmune symptoms appear.

keyConcept: In adult males and postmenopausal women, iron deficiency anemia is most commonly due to chronic GI blood loss, and evaluation should focus on identifying ulcers or malignancy through appropriate endoscopy. Always treat IDA in men as a potential sign of GI cancer until ruled out.

diagram.name: Microcytic Anemia – Iron Deficiency Anemia in Adult Males (Chronic GI Blood Loss Focus)
diagram.caption: This diagram illustrates iron deficiency anemia in adult males, emphasizing microcytic, hypochromic RBCs and characteristic lab findings (low ferritin, high TIBC). It highlights chronic gastrointestinal blood loss—such as from peptic ulcers and colorectal malignancy—as the most common cause. The flow also demonstrates the diagnostic approach, including fecal occult blood testing and endoscopy, stressing the need to rule out GI malignancy.
